mainTopic: When a side post that is visible only from outside counts as a לחי, and how לבוד applies to rows of posts and to a breached courtyard.
overview: This amud explains when a side post (לחי) counts for permitting carrying in an alley. רב אשי explains the מחלוקת about לבוד as a case of posts lined up with gaps under four טפחים for four אמות. According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the posts join into a wall that forms its own מבוי, so it needs another לחי. According to the רבנן, it does not. The row of posts cannot serve as its own לחי, because רבי יוחנן rules that a post 'visible from outside, flush inside' is not a לחי. The גמרא then shows that רבי חייא, who taught a ברייתא saying such a post does count, holds the opposite view. A sage who teaches a ruling is assumed to agree with it. רבה בר רב הונא rules like רבי חייא. He is challenged from the משנה of a small courtyard breached into a large one. רבי זירא, רבינא and the גמרא then debate whether לבוד can close the gaps around the opening. The amud ends with the question of whether לבוד on one side alone is enough.

steps.title: רב אשי describes a new case: an alley lined with side posts
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי offers a different case to explain the מחלוקת. Someone lined the alley with side posts, each gap under four טפחים, for a length of four אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: For example, where someone lined it with side posts, each less than four handbreadths apart, for a length of four cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a new, different explanation of what case the earlier מחלוקת is about. He describes a row of side posts with small gaps between them, running four אמות long.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier explanations placed the מחלוקת in a different case. רב אשי moves it to a row of posts with gaps of less than four טפחים, because that gap size is exactly where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן disagree about לבוד. The four-אמות length matters because a stretch that long can count as its own alley.

keyTerms.meaning: he lined it / filled it in a row
side posts (plural of לֶחִי)
each one less than four (טפחים) apart
over a length of four cubits

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
for example, where one lined it with side posts
each less than four (handbreadths) apart
phrases.notes: The gap between each post and the next is under four טפחים.

phrases.english: for a length of four cubits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative explanation to the earlier explanations of רבי יוחנן's statement, which appear on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מחלוקת is about an alley lined with posts spaced less than four טפחים apart, running four אמות long.

steps.title: How each side rules in רב אשי's case
steps.stepSummary: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, לבוד joins the posts into one wall, which makes a separate מבוי that needs another לחי. According to the רבנן, there is no לבוד, so no extra לחי is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who says we apply לבוד, it is an alleyway and needs another side post to permit it. According to the רבנן, who say we do not apply לבוד, it does not need another side post to permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי now shows how his case fits each opinion. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says it needs an extra לחי, and the רבנן say it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applies לבוד to gaps under four טפחים, so all the posts merge into one solid wall four אמות long. A stretch like that counts as its own alley and needs its own לחי. The רבנן only apply לבוד to gaps under three טפחים, so the posts stay separate and never form a new alley.

keyTerms.meaning: the rule that a small gap is treated as closed, joining two things
we say / we apply
an alleyway
another side post
to permit it (for carrying)

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree that לבוד exists. They only argue about the size of the gap: under four טפחים for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, under three for the רבנן. The gaps in this case fall in between.

phrases.english: According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who said:
we apply lavud (for gaps under four)
it becomes an alleyway (of its own),
and it needs another side post to permit it.
And according to the Rabbis, who say:
we do not apply lavud (unless the gap is under three)
it does not need another side post to permit it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל דְּאָמַר: אָמְרִינַן לָבוּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב אשי's case to each of the two opinions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, an extra לחי is required. According to the רבנן, it is not.

steps.title: Why not treat the row as a valid side post?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's ruling. The row should count as a לחי that is 'visible from outside and even from inside,' so no extra לחי should be needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, let it be like a post that is visible from the outside and even from the inside!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires another לחי at all. The row of posts should itself work as the לחי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the outside, the row can be seen as a side post. From the inside, it looks even with the alley wall. If a post like that counts as a לחי, then the row already does the job, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's demand for 'another' לחי seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: let it be (treated as)
visible (as a side post) from the outside
even (flush) with the wall from the inside

phrases.english: And according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
let it be like (a post) visible from the outside
and even from the inside!
phrases.notes: A post like that should count as a לחי, so no extra one is needed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרִבֵּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, לֶהֱוֵי כְּנִרְאֶה מִבַּחוּץ וְשָׁוֶה מִבִּפְנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling given for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, another לחי is required.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The row itself should qualify as a 'visible from outside, even from inside' לחי, which would make an additional לחי unnecessary.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן holds such a post does not count
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי's explanation follows רבי יוחנן. As רבין reported, רבי יוחנן rules that a post 'visible from outside, even from inside' is not treated as a לחי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't the reasoning only according to רבי יוחנן? And when רבין came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: A post visible from the outside and even from the inside is not considered a side post.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רב אשי is explaining רבי יוחנן's view, and רבי יוחנן rules that this kind of post does not count as a לחי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that a 'visible from outside, even from inside' post works as a לחי. רבי יוחנן, as reported by רבין, rejects that, and the whole discussion is according to רבי יוחנן. So the row cannot serve as its own לחי, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל correctly requires another one.

keyTerms.meaning: isn't the reasoning only (according to...)?
when רבין came (from ארץ ישראל)
it is not judged / not treated as
as a side post

steps.confusionAlert: 'מידי הוא טעמא אלא' sounds like a question, but it is really a statement: 'This reasoning only follows רבי יוחנן, doesn't it?'
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב אשי, the מחלוקת is about posts with gaps under four טפחים running four אמות. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires another לחי, and the row cannot count as its own לחי, because רבי יוחנן rules that a 'visible from outside, even from inside' post is not a לחי.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that an explanation must stay consistent with the אמורא it is explaining. Because רב אשי is explaining רבי יוחנן, רבי יוחנן's other rulings limit what the case can mean.

phrases.english: Isn't the reasoning
only according to Rabbi Yochanan?
Didn't Ravin, when he came,
say that Rabbi Yochanan said:
(a post) visible from the outside and even from the inside
is not considered a side post.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִידֵּי הוּא טַעְמָא אֶלָּא לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the challenge's assumption by citing the אמורא whose view is being explained
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A post 'visible from outside, even from inside' should count as a לחי, so the row would permit itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי יוחנן, such a post is not a לחי, so another לחי is truly needed according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.title: A recorded dispute about a post that sticks out on only one side
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees: a post that sticks out on the inside of the alley but is flush on the outside counts as a לחי. For the opposite case, sticking out on the outside but flush on the inside, רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי argue. One says it counts as a לחי and one says it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: if a post is visible from inside and even (flush) from outside, it is judged as a לחי. If it is visible from outside and flush from inside, רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי argue. One said it is judged as a לחי, and the other said it is not judged as a לחי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an earlier dispute between two sages about the exact type of post that רבי יוחנן just ruled on. It is setting up the next move: figuring out which sage holds which view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two cases. A post that is visible from the inside counts as a לחי, with no argument. The only argument is about a post that is visible only from the outside, which is the case רבי יוחנן disqualified. The text here does not say which sage takes which side. The next step works that out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was stated.' This introduces a dispute or ruling among אמוראים.
Visible from inside, meaning it sticks out on the side facing into the alley.
Flush or even from outside, so it does not stand out on that side.
It is judged as (has the status of) a לחי.
'One said... and the other said.' Two views are given without saying who holds which.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. 'Visible from inside' counts for everyone. Only 'visible from outside, flush inside' is in dispute, and that is the case רבי יוחנן disqualified.

phrases.english: It was stated:
If it is visible from inside and even (flush) from outside,
it is judged as a side post.
If it is visible from outside and flush from inside,
phrases.notes: This is the case רבי יוחנן ruled on in the previous step.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi disagree:
one said: it is judged as a side post,

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד אָמַר: אֵינוֹ נִידּוֹן מִשּׁוּם לֶחִי.
phrases.english: and the other said: it is not judged as a side post.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings in an older dispute about the same case רבי יוחנן ruled on in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Visible from inside counts as a לחי. Visible only from outside is disputed between רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי.

steps.title: Proving that רבי חייא is the one who says it counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבי חייא is the one who says the post counts as a לחי. The evidence is his own ברייתא, which says that a recessed wall counts as a לחי whichever side the recess is visible from.
steps.simpleTranslation: Conclude that רבי חייא is the one who said 'it is judged as a לחי.' For רבי חייא taught: a wall whose one side is recessed more than the other, whether the recess is visible from outside and flush from inside, or visible from inside and flush from outside, is judged as a לחי. Conclude so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to figure out which sage holds which view in the dispute. It points to a ברייתא that רבי חייא himself taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's ברייתא explicitly includes the case of 'visible from outside, flush from inside' and says it counts as a לחי. So it seems that רבי חייא is the lenient sage in the dispute, and רבי שמעון ברבי is the strict one.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Conclude' or 'let it be determined.' This introduces a proof that identifies who holds which view.
'For he taught.' It introduces a ברייתא that the sage taught.
Recessed, set back.
'Whether... or.' It means both cases are included.

phrases.english: Conclude that Rabbi Chiya
is the one who said 'it is judged as a side post,'
for Rabbi Chiya taught:
a wall that has one side more recessed than the other,
whether it is visible from outside and flush from inside,
or it is visible from inside and flush from outside,
it is judged as a side post.
Conclude so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles which sage holds which view in the dispute from step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי חייא is the one who rules the post counts as a לחי.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חייא's own ברייתא about a recessed wall, which includes the case 'visible from outside, flush from inside.'

steps.title: Challenge: maybe רבי חייא knew the ruling but did not follow it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. רבי יוחנן surely knew this famous ruling, yet he ruled against it. So knowing a ruling does not mean agreeing with it, and maybe רבי חייא also did not agree with it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And did רבי יוחנן not hear this? Rather, he heard it and did not hold by it. Then רבי חייא also may not hold by it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof from the last step. It argues that a sage can know a ruling without agreeing with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן ruled (step 4) that this kind of post is not a לחי, even though he must have known this well-known ruling. That shows a ruling can be known but rejected. If so, the fact that רבי חייא knew the ruling does not prove he held by it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Did he not hear it?' A rhetorical question meaning he certainly heard it.
He does not hold by it, meaning he does not agree with it.
Also.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִי לָא שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ הָא?!
phrases.english: And did Rabbi Yochanan not hear this?!

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ וְלָא סָבַר לַהּ,
phrases.english: Rather, he heard it and does not hold by it;

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חִיָּיא נָמֵי לָא סָבַר לַהּ!
phrases.english: so Rabbi Chiya too may not hold by it!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִי לָא שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ הָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from step 6 by using רבי יוחנן's position from step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof that identifies רבי חייא as the lenient sage, not the ruling of the ברייתא itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Knowing a ruling does not mean agreeing with it, as רבי יוחנן's case shows.

steps.title: Answer: nobody teaches a ruling he rejects
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. רבי יוחנן did not hold by the ruling, and that is why he did not teach it. רבי חייא did teach it, and there would be no reason to teach it if he rejected it. So the proof stands: רבי חייא holds that the post counts as a לחי.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this comparison? It makes sense that רבי יוחנן did not hold by it, and that is why he did not teach it. But רבי חייא, if he did not hold by it, why would he teach it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and shows that the comparison between רבי יוחנן and רבי חייא does not work. With that, the proof from step 6 is restored.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a big difference between hearing a ruling and teaching it. רבי יוחנן only heard it, so he could reject it. רבי חייא actually taught it as his own ברייתא, which shows he agreed with it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is this?' It rejects a comparison as not valid.
'It is fine for... but...' It contrasts a case that makes sense with one that does not.
'Why would he need to teach it?'
'If it were so.'

steps.whatToRemember: The disputed case is a post visible from outside but flush inside. רבי חייא holds that it counts as a לחי, because he taught it in his ברייתא. רבי יוחנן holds that it does not count.
steps.whyThisMatters: This uses a common principle in the גמרא: a sage who teaches a ruling is assumed to agree with it. That principle lets the גמרא settle who holds which side when a dispute is recorded with 'one said... and the other said.'

phrases.english: What is this comparison?!

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לָא סָבַר לַהּ —
phrases.english: It makes sense that Rabbi Yochanan does not hold by it;
that is why he does not teach it.
But Rabbi Chiya,
if it were so that he does not hold by it,
why would he need to teach it?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי מַאי?! בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לָא סָבַר לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 7 and restores the proof of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the two cases: hearing a ruling versus teaching it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רבי יוחנן knew the ruling and rejected it, רבי חייא might also have known it and rejected it.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי חייא taught the ruling, so he must agree with it. He is the one who says the post counts as a לחי.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי חייא holds that a post visible from outside and flush inside counts as a לחי.

steps.title: A post visible outside but flush inside counts as a לחי
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא rules that a post that sticks out on the outside but is flush on the inside does count as a לחי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: If a post is visible from the outside but flush (even with the wall) on the inside, it is treated as a לחי.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא gives a clear ruling on the case that was disputed earlier: the post that sticks out only on the outside counts as a לחי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי argued about exactly this case, and the גמרא showed that רבי חייא is the one who says it counts. רבה בר רב הונא now states that lenient position as a plain rule. The next steps will test it against a משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Visible from the outside, meaning the post sticks out when seen from outside the alley
Even (flush) on the inside, meaning from inside the alley it looks like part of the wall
It is judged as a לחי, the side post that makes carrying in an alley permitted

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
If it is visible from the outside and even on the inside —
it is treated as a side post (לחי).
phrases.notes: This matches the view the גמרא attributed to רבי חייא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a definite ruling on the case that רבי חייא and רבי שמעון ברבי disputed, matching רבי חייא's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A post visible from outside but flush from inside counts as a לחי.

steps.title: Challenge from the small courtyard breached into a large courtyard
steps.stepSummary: רבה reports that the בית מדרש challenged this rule from a משנה. A small courtyard breached into a large one is forbidden for carrying, even though it seems to be a 'visible outside, flush inside' case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: We raised an objection against our ruling. A small courtyard whose wall broke open into a large courtyard: in the large one carrying is permitted, and in the small one it is forbidden, because the opening is like a doorway of the large one. If the ruling is true, the small one should also be permitted, since it is a case of 'visible from outside and flush inside'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה בר רב הונא's rule using a משנה about two courtyards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The small courtyard's entire wall is gone, so from inside it there is no wall stub at all. That is the 'flush inside' part. From the large courtyard, though, the large courtyard's wall pieces on both sides of the opening are visible. That is the 'visible outside' part. By רבה בר רב הונא's rule the small courtyard should be permitted, yet the משנה forbids it.

keyTerms.meaning: We raised an objection against our own ruling
A courtyard whose wall was breached (broken open)
Like a doorway of the large courtyard
And if it is so, meaning if the ruling is correct (a standard opening for a challenge)
It should be permitted

steps.confusionAlert: Picture it carefully. The small courtyard has lost its ENTIRE wall facing the large one, so it has nothing standing at its opening. The large courtyard has lost only part of its wall, so wall pieces remain on both sides of the opening. That is why the opening is 'flush' from the small side but 'visible' from the large side.

phrases.english: Rabba said: And we raised an objection against our ruling:
A small courtyard that was breached into a large one —
the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden,
because it is like a doorway of the large one.
And if it is so, the small one should also be permitted
because of 'visible from outside and even on the inside.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 9 from a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר רב הונא's rule that 'visible outside, flush inside' counts as a לחי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The small courtyard in the משנה fits 'visible outside, flush inside', yet the משנה forbids carrying there. So the rule seems to be wrong.

steps.title: The small courtyard's walls stick into the large one
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains that the משנה describes a layout where the small courtyard's walls stick into the large courtyard. In that layout, nothing visible from outside frames the opening.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: The משנה is talking about a case where the walls of the small courtyard extend into the large one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא defends the rule by saying the משנה is about a special layout that is not a 'visible outside' case at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the small courtyard's side walls push into the large courtyard, its opening is not lined up with the large courtyard's wall. The large courtyard's leftover wall pieces then do not frame the opening, so nothing is 'visible from outside'. The משנה forbids the small courtyard for that reason, and the rule stays intact.

keyTerms.meaning: Entering, here meaning sticking into or extending into
The walls of

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
It is a case where the walls of the small one extend into the large one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 by narrowing the case of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the משנה describes a specific physical layout.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה describes a plain 'visible outside, flush inside' case, which would contradict the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the משנה's layout, the small courtyard's walls stick into the large one, so nothing visible from outside frames the opening. The משנה does not contradict the rule.

steps.title: Why not close the gap with לבוד?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even in רבי זירא's layout, let לבוד connect the small courtyard's walls to the large courtyard's wall. Then the small courtyard would be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And let us say לבוד, and the small courtyard should be permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי זירא's answer by bringing in the rule of לבוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לבוד says that a small gap counts as closed. If the gap between the small courtyard's walls and the large courtyard's wall is small, we should treat them as connected. Then the large courtyard's wall would again frame the opening from outside, and the small courtyard should be permitted after all.

keyTerms.meaning: The rule that a gap of less than three טפחים is treated as closed, as if the two pieces are joined
And let us say (introduces a suggested reasoning)

phrases.english: And let us say lavud, and it should be permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי זירא's answer from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's explanation that the walls of the small courtyard stick into the large one.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With לבוד, the small gap disappears and the opening is framed from outside again. So the small courtyard should be permitted, and רבי זירא's layout does not explain why the משנה forbids it.

steps.title: Blocking the reply that the gaps are too wide
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks a possible defense: maybe the gaps are too wide for לבוד. A ברייתא shows the משנה applies even when the courtyards differ by only one אמה, which leaves tiny gaps.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the walls are far apart (too far for לבוד), didn't רב אדא בר אבימי teach before רבי חנינא: the small courtyard can be ten אמות wide and the large one eleven?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא strengthens its challenge by shutting down the obvious reply that the gaps are too big for לבוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא says the משנה's law applies even when the large courtyard is only one אמה wider than the small one. One אמה is six טפחים. If the small courtyard sits in the middle, only about three טפחים are left on each side, which is small enough for לבוד. So the 'too far apart' defense fails, and the challenge stands for now.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (introduces an expected answer in order to reject it)
They are very far apart
But didn't he teach? (introduces a source that refutes the suggestion)
Before (in the presence of) someone

steps.whatToRemember: רבה בר רב הונא says 'visible outside, flush inside' counts as a לחי. The courtyard משנה seems to contradict this. רבי זירא's answer, that the small courtyard's walls stick into the large one, is now under attack: לבוד should close the small gaps, and the ברייתא of ten and eleven אמות shows the gaps can be tiny.

phrases.english: And if you say that they are very far apart?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא תָּנֵי רַב אַדָּא בַּר אֲבִימִי
phrases.english: But didn't Rav Adda bar Avimi teach
before Rabbi Ḥanina:
The small one, at ten (אמות).
The large one, at eleven!
phrases.notes: A difference of one אמה (six טפחים) leaves about three טפחים on each side, which is in the range of לבוד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reinforces the לבוד challenge of step 12 by ruling out the defense that the gaps are too wide.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible defense of רבי זירא that the gaps are too wide for לבוד.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows the משנה applies even with a one-אמה difference, so the gaps can be small enough for לבוד. The 'too far apart' defense cannot save רבי זירא's answer.

steps.title: רבינא: the gaps are uneven, two handbreadths on one side and four on the other
steps.stepSummary: רבינא defends the משנה by saying the six טפחים of difference are split unevenly. One side has a gap of two טפחים and the other has a gap of four. The four-טפח gap is too wide for לבוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The case is where the small courtyard's walls are set apart from this wall of the big courtyard by two טפחים, and from that other wall of the big courtyard by four טפחים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge from Step 13. He shows how a one-אמה difference can still leave a gap too wide for לבוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One אמה is six טפחים. The challenge in Step 13 assumed the small courtyard sits evenly in the middle, which leaves about three טפחים on each side, close enough for לבוד. רבינא answers that the small courtyard does not have to be centered. The six טפחים can be split two on one side and four on the other, and the four-טפח side is too wide for לבוד.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer in this step
Separated, set apart (the walls are a distance away)
Wall
Handbreadth; six of them make one אמה

steps.confusionAlert: The numbers two and four are טפחים, not אמות. Together they add up to six טפחים, which is exactly the one אמה difference from the ברייתא in Step 13.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
It is where they are set apart from this wall by two handbreadths,
phrases.notes: The small courtyard's wall is two טפחים away from one wall of the big courtyard. This is close enough for לבוד.

phrases.english: and from this other wall by four handbreadths.
phrases.notes: This gap is four טפחים, too wide for לבוד, so this side stays open.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: בְּמוּפְלָגִין מִכּוֹתֶל זֶה בִּשְׁנַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 13's claim that a one-אמה difference leaves gaps small enough for לבוד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case's physical layout (an uneven split of the gap)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A one-אמה difference must leave small gaps on both sides that לבוד can close, so the small courtyard should be permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: The six טפחים can be split two and four. The four-טפח side cannot be closed by לבוד, so the משנה's ruling still holds.

steps.title: Let the narrow two-handbreadth side work on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבינא. Even if only one side is close enough for לבוד, that one side should be enough to permit the small courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us say לבוד works from one side, and the small courtyard should be permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבינא's answer. It argues that the two-טפח side still allows לבוד, and one side might be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא only showed that one side cannot use לבוד. The other side, at two טפחים, still can. If לבוד on a single side is enough to frame the opening, the small courtyard should be permitted after all, so רבינא's layout does not yet explain the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: But let us say (a challenge opener)
From one side or direction
And it should be permitted

phrases.english: But let us say lavud applies from one side, and it should be permitted.
phrases.notes: The two-טפח gap can be closed by לבוד, so the opening is framed on that side at least.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's answer in Step 14 as not going far enough.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's explanation that the uneven gaps keep the small courtyard forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבינא's layout still leaves one gap of two טפחים, which לבוד can close. If framing on one side is enough, the small courtyard should be permitted, which contradicts the משנה.
